strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting reformulation of video object removal as video-to-video translation using a stochastic bridge, replacing the standard noise-to-data diffusion paradigm with a direct source-to-target bridge that leverages the input video as a structural prior.

The use of a VP-SDE bridge with an analytic ternary interpolation and velocity-matching objective is technically plausible and may provide a simpler training scheme than simulating stochastic paths directly.
The adaptive mask modulation (AMM) strategy is simple and well-motivated, aiming to balance background fidelity against generative flexibility for large occlusions.
The qualitative results in Figures 2-4 are visually promising: the method appears to preserve background detail, maintain temporal consistency, and even remove associated shadows outside the mask.
The training dataset construction is relatively large-scale and attempts to cover both synthetic and real dynamic-object scenarios using SAM2 and Qwen3-VL filtering.
The impact statement briefly acknowledges potential misuse risks of video object removal technology.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim that the method 'significantly outperforms' existing methods is not supported by any quantitative evaluation. There are no tables, no PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD/temporal-consistency metrics, no benchmark results, no user study, and no statistical comparisons.

The 'Extensive experiments' claimed in the abstract and conclusion reduce to a few qualitative comparison figures. This is insufficient for an ICML main-track contribution and prevents reliable assessment of the method's actual performance.

There is no ablation study for the proposed adaptive mask modulation, the bridge formulation, the dual-role conditioning of z_src, or the VP-SDE parameterization. The contributions cannot be isolated or validated.

The qualitative comparison lacks a clear evaluation protocol: the test set, number of videos, baseline configurations, prompt settings, and selection criteria are not described, raising concerns about cherry-picking and unfair comparison.

Several technical details are incomplete or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 line 9 contains a typo ('u_t = u_t/rho_t epsilon ...' instead of using a_t), Eq. 13 is not clearly justified, and the inference weights w1,w2,w3 in Eq. 14 are never specified.

The training objective refers to an Appendix for the velocity derivation, but no Appendix is present in the manuscript. Key theoretical claims about the bridge process, the tractable h term, and the score relation are therefore not fully verifiable.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model release is mentioned, baseline implementation details are missing, random seeds/compute budget are only partially reported, and the exact evaluation data are unspecified.

The AMM description is unclear in practice: it is not explained how the binary mask M is aligned with DiT patch embeddings, how the VAE-encoded mask z_M is used, or where exactly the modulation is applied within the transformer blocks.

The paper does not discuss limitations or failure cases. It does not address performance on very large objects, long videos, dynamic camera motion, computational cost, or domain gaps introduced by the composite training data.

The evaluation does not use standard video object removal/inpainting benchmarks, making it difficult to compare with published results or to judge generalization beyond the authors' qualitative examples.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and practically important task (video object removal) and proposes a coherent high-level pipeline: encoding source/target/mask into a VAE latent space and training a DiT backbone (initialized from Wan2.1-1.3B) under a bridge/velocity-matching objective.

Reformulating object removal as a video-to-video (data-to-data) translation rather than noise-to-data generation is intuitively appealing, and leveraging the input video as a structural prior is a reasonable motivation.

The qualitative figures (Figs. 2-4) suggest the method can produce plausible backgrounds and, interestingly, sometimes removes shadows not included in the mask, which is a potentially useful behavior worth investigating.
The training setup is described with concrete details (81 frames, bucket-based multi-resolution, 8xH100, AdamW, 50-step inference), and a large 47k-pair dataset is assembled.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method 'significantly outperforms existing methods in both visual quality and temporal consistency' is entirely unsupported: the Experiments section reports no quantitative metrics at all (no PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, no FVD/VFID, no temporal-consistency metric, no user study). The claim of 'extensive experiments' is therefore misleading, as only a handful of qualitative figures are shown. This is a fundamental evidential gap.

No ablation studies are provided. Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) is presented as a core contribution, yet there is no experiment isolating its effect, so the claim that it 'balances background fidelity with generative flexibility' is unverified.

AMM (Eq. 15) is far less sophisticated than advertised. It is h' = h ⊙ (M + (1-M)(1+γ)) with a single learnable scalar γ initialized to zero, i.e., a global multiplicative rescaling of background embeddings. This is not 'dynamic' modulation conditioned on 'mask characteristics'; the description in the abstract/intro overstates the mechanism, and it does not adapt per region, scale, or occlusion size.

Originality is limited. The bridge/VP-SDE formulation (ternary interpolation, coefficients a_t,b_t,c_t, bridge score guidance) closely follows existing work (Zhou et al. 2023a DDBM; Liu et al. 2023 I2SB; Wang et al. 2025 FrameBridge for I2V). The contribution reduces to applying an existing bridge model to video object removal plus a trivial scalar embedding scaling.

Technical inconsistencies and sloppiness in the core equations. Eq. 11 defines u_t = (a_t/ρ_t)ε - (c_t/ρ_t)z_tgt, but Algorithm 1 step 9 writes u_t = (u_t/ρ_t)ε - (c_t/ρ_t)z_tgt (a typo). Inverting Eq. 11 to recover ẑ_{0|t} (Eq. 13) appears to omit a ρ_t factor (the algebra yields ρ_t v̂_t, not v̂_t), and the derivation of the velocity target and solver weights is deferred to an appendix not available for verification.

Notation is inconsistent and the exposition is error-prone: the bridge uses both T and 1 as the endpoint (Eq. 7 vs. Eq. 9/10), Eq. 7's 'z_0 ~ p_data' is ambiguous about which endpoint it is, and the text contains broken sentences ('leading to leading to incomplete object erasure...').

Reproducibility is weak: no code or data release is mentioned, no evaluation protocol or baseline inference settings are specified, and it is unclear whether baselines were given fair compute/steps, making the qualitative comparisons hard to trust.

There is no limitations discussion, despite the abstract/intro making strong claims; the observed 'implicit shadow removal' is neither quantified nor analyzed, and the compositing-based training data (SAM2 + Qwen3-VL filtering) may introduce a realism gap that is not examined.

The motivation that noise-to-data diffusion is 'suboptimal' is argued only qualitatively and is not substantiated with any controlled comparison, so the premise driving the method is itself unverified.

strengths: Reformulates video object removal as a video-to-video translation task using a stochastic bridge, which is a sensible and potentially impactful shift away from noise-to-data diffusion inpainting.

The adaptive mask modulation idea is intuitive: scaling background embeddings while preserving object-region features could help balance source-video fidelity and generative flexibility for large occlusions.
The paper builds on a strong pre-trained video DiT backbone (Wan2.1-1.3B) and constructs a large training corpus (~47k video pairs), indicating substantial engineering effort.
Qualitative figures suggest the method can produce plausible backgrounds and may implicitly remove shadows outside the mask, which is a promising capability compared with mask-dependent baselines.
The impact statement acknowledges potential misuse risks of video object removal.
weaknesses: The paper contains no quantitative evaluation. The experiments section only presents qualitative comparisons, with no PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, VFID, temporal-consistency metrics, benchmark tables, or user study. The central claim that the method 'significantly outperforms existing methods' is therefore unsupported.

There are no ablation studies. The proposed adaptive mask modulation (AMM) is not ablated, nor is the bridge formulation compared against standard noise-to-data diffusion. The key claimed mechanism remains empirically unvalidated.

The mathematical formulation has inconsistencies. Eq. 12 trains vθ to approximate u_t, but Eq. 13 inverts the relation as if vθ = ρ_t u_t (or has a missing factor of ρ_t). Algorithm 1 line 9 also contains a typo ('u_t = u_t/ρ_t ε - c_t/ρ_t z_tgt') and omits the b_t z_src term. Eq. 7 uses z_T = z_src while training uses t ∈ [0,1] and z_1 = z_src. These errors undermine soundness and reproducibility.

The inference solver is incompletely specified. Eq. 14 states that weights w1, w2, w3 are analytically determined, but they are never defined. The condition injection mechanism for y in the DiT is also not described in enough detail to reproduce.
Reproducibility is limited: no code is provided, evaluation datasets and splits are not specified, baseline configurations are not reported, and key architecture/training details are missing.

The paper lacks a limitations section. It does not discuss failure cases, computational cost, memory requirements, inference latency, dependence on the pre-trained Wan model, or sensitivity to mask quality.
Evaluation is not performed on standard video object removal benchmarks. Only a few selected qualitative clips are shown, making it impossible to assess generalization or statistical significance.
Dataset construction uses real human-centric videos processed with SAM2 and Qwen3-VL, but there is no discussion of privacy, consent, licensing, or dataset bias.

Originality is incremental: the method largely adapts existing bridge models and a pre-trained video DiT. The claimed 'novel adaptive mask modulation' is a simple feature-scaling heuristic without theoretical analysis or empirical justification.

strengths: The core framing—reformulating video object removal as a video-to-video translation via a stochastic (VP-SDE) bridge rather than noise-to-data diffusion—is well motivated and sensible. Using the input video latent as the prior boundary (z_src) and simultaneously as a spatial condition is a reasonable way to exploit structural priors.

Quantitative results are competitive: on both DAVIS and BridgeRemoval-Bench the method achieves best or second-best across all reported metrics, and notably best CLIP-F, PSNR and MSE on both datasets, plus a favorable runtime of 1.111 s/frame versus most baselines.

The paper introduces BridgeRemoval-Bench, a 150-video benchmark spanning landscape/portrait, single/multiple objects, and multiple sources (stock, synthetic via Veo, in-the-wild social media), which is a potentially useful community contribution given the acknowledged scale/diversity limits of DAVIS and ROSE-Bench.
A user study (24 participants, 1440 evaluations) across textual consistency, background fidelity, and temporal consistency provides complementary evidence favoring the method.
The limitation discussion (Appendix E, fast-moving objects) is honest and situates the failure mode as a field-wide challenge rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The central claim that the bridge formulation yields superior object removal is not validated by a controlled ablation. The paper compares only against external methods that differ in base architecture, training data, conditioning, and objectives. There is no apples-to-apples experiment isolating the bridge formulation (e.g., the same DiT, same data, same y=Concat(z_M, z_src) conditioning, trained with standard flow matching vs. the bridge). Table 3 asserts the distinction but provides no empirical comparison, so the decisive evidence for the paper's main hypothesis is missing.

The claim of 'significantly outperforms' is overstated. On the metric most directly tied to whether the object was actually removed (CLIP-T), the method is never best: on DAVIS it is 0.2788 vs. GenOmnimatte 0.2814, and on BridgeRemoval-Bench 0.2922 vs. GenOmnimatte 0.2966. The PSNR gain on BridgeRemoval-Bench (1.64 dB) is the only clearly large margin, and several other gaps (LPIPS vs. VACE) are small or negative.

Technical novelty is limited: the training objective, marginal coefficients, and reverse process are explicitly adapted from DDBM, and AMM is essentially a FiLM-style mask-conditioned modulation. The contribution is therefore largely an application/engineering transfer rather than a new method.
The AMM ablation is purely qualitative (a single bus example in Figure 4); no quantitative ablation of AMM is provided, despite AMM being listed as a core contribution.

Inconsistency/ambiguity in AMM: Eq. 5 encodes the mask as z_M = E(M) for conditioning, but Eq. 15 feeds the raw mask M into a learnable 3D-conv patch embedding φ_M. It is unclear whether AMM operates on the raw mask or the VAE latent, where in the DiT stack the modulation is inserted, and how it interacts with the concatenated z_M condition.

Reproducibility gaps: the SDE solver weights w_1, w_2, w_3 are described only as 'analytically determined' and never given, so the reverse process cannot be reproduced. The project page/reference URLs appear to be missing ('The project page is', 'More samples can be visited at:'), and no code release is stated. Training is also only 20k steps, with no compute/ablation details on schedule sensitivity.

The Appendix B derivations are somewhat hand-wavy. The mapping from the general DDBM coefficients (Eq. 22) to the specific σ-based parameterization (Eq. 23) is asserted ('this equality holds if we define the underlying diffusion schedule such that...') rather than rigorously derived, and the argument invoking α_T ≈ 0 and SNR_T ≈ 0 sits uneasily with a bridge that must terminate exactly at z_src.

Evaluation methodology concerns: CLIP-T between the output and a Qwen3-VL-generated caption of the clean video is a weak proxy for verifying object removal; caption similarity can be high even when the object remains, and vice versa. The benchmark itself is captioned by the same Qwen3-VL pipeline, which may bias the metric toward methods matching the caption distribution.

Presentation quality is rough: repeated text ('leading to leading to'), incomplete sentences, mismatched figure/table captions (e.g., Figure 4 caption references the bus example shown in Appendix C), and an apparent GPU typo ('L20X'). The impact statement does not address the ethics of the training pipeline, which composites SAM2-extracted real-world foregrounds (potentially identifiable people) and includes scraped TikTok footage with unclear licensing/consent.

strengths: Reasonable and well-motivated reformulation: casting video object removal as video-to-video translation with a VP-SDE bridge and a Dirac prior δ_{z_src} is a sensible, practically relevant direction, and the observation that noise-initialized inpainting is awkward for removal (incomplete erasure / hallucinated content) is a legitimate gap.

Competitive empirical results: best PSNR/MSE on both DAVIS and BridgeRemoval-Bench, best CLIP-F on their benchmark, +1.64 dB PSNR over prior SOTA on BridgeRemoval-Bench, at a lower per-frame runtime (1.111 s/frame) than most baselines.

A new benchmark (BridgeRemoval-Bench, 150 videos spanning stock/synthetic/in-the-wild sources, portrait and landscape, single and multi-object, SAM2 masks plus captions) is a genuine community resource that addresses real limitations of DAVIS and ROSE-Bench.

Useful supporting evidence: AMM ablation on a large-object (bus) case (Fig. 4), inference-step study (Table 4, Fig. 5) showing 10 steps already yields best PSNR/CLIP-F, and a user study with 24 participants / 1440 ratings.

The implementation pipeline is largely self-consistent: I verified that Eq. 13 (ẑ_{0|t} = (a_t/ρ_t²)z_t − (a_t b_t/ρ_t²)z_src − (c_t/ρ_t)v̂_t) correctly inverts the reparameterization z_t = a_t z_tgt + b_t z_src + c_t ε with u_t as defined, and the algorithmic listings are readable.
The limitations section is honest: it explicitly acknowledges failures on fast-moving objects and notes that ROSE/VACE/GenOmnimatte share the same failure mode.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially DDBM (Zhou et al., 2023a) transferred to video inpainting on top of a Wan2.1-1.3B backbone: the coefficients a_t = σ̄_t²/σ_1², b_t = σ_t²/σ_1², c_t = σ̄_t σ_t/σ_1 are the standard bridge coefficients, and Appendix B.1 concedes 'our method strictly adheres to the DDBM theoretical framework.' AMM is a FiLM/SPADE-style mask-conditioned scale-and-shift, not a new mechanism.

The central theoretical derivation is circular and internally inconsistent. Appendix B.1 claims the specific coefficients are 'recovered' from the general DDBM form (A_t, B_t, C_t) merely because 'this equality holds if we define the underlying diffusion schedule such that the SNR ratio matches our variance schedule,' and then states 'α_T ≈ 0 (so SNR_T ≈ 0)' — which would zero out B_t = (SNR_T/SNR_t)(α_t/α_T) and collapse the bridge to a standard diffusion model, contradicting the bridge itself. The mapping is asserted, not proven; B.2 and B.3 similarly assert rather than derive.

No controlled ablation for the paper's central claim. There is no experiment comparing bridge vs. flow matching / noise-to-data with the identical backbone, data, and training budget, even though Appendix A (Table 3) sets up exactly this comparison. The main evidence is a comparison to ROSE, which was trained by its authors with a different recipe and data, so the causal claim that the bridge formulation drives the gains is not established.

The motivating premise is overstated. Modern diffusion inpainting baselines (VACE, DiffuEraser, BrushNet-style) already condition on the masked input video, so the assertion that noise-to-data methods 'discard' the input video's priors is inaccurate; the real difference is initialization-from-z_src vs. conditioning-on-z_src, and the paper never isolates that.
Relevant SOTA baselines are cited but never compared: DiffuEraser (Li et al., 2025b) and MiniMax-Remover (Zi et al., 2025a) are both described as state-of-the-art yet are absent from Tables 1 and 2.

Claims exceed the evidence. The abstract/conclusion claim the method 'significantly outperforms existing methods,' but on DAVIS CLIP-T the method scores 0.2788 vs GenOmnimatte's 0.2814, and on BridgeRemoval-Bench CLIP-T 0.2922 vs GenOmnimatte's 0.2966 — i.e., it does not lead on the very metric used to measure object removal. Many margins are tiny (CLIP-F 0.9917 vs 0.9887) with no variance or significance testing, and the 'best or second best' hedge in the text is much weaker than the abstract's claim.

Metric design confers a partly trivial advantage. PSNR/MSE/LPIPS are computed only on unmasked regions while z_src is both the bridge start point and an explicit concatenated condition, so preserving non-masked areas is nearly free; high PSNR there is weak evidence of quality yet is the headline result.

Reproducibility gaps. The SDE solver weights w1, w2, w3 in Eq. 14 / Algorithm 2 are described only as 'analytically determined by the bridge schedule' and are never given, making the inference procedure unreproducible. AMM's insertion point (which DiT blocks/layers) is unspecified; F_M = φ_M(M) is described as a learnable patch embedding at latent resolution while the mask is also VAE-encoded into z_M, and the relationship between the two mask pathways is unclear. No code/weights release is indicated and the project page is blank.

Benchmark construction and evaluation protocol are underspecified. CLIP-T is computed against Qwen3-VL captions of the object-removed video, but it is unclear how such captions were produced when the target video does not exist; if they are derived from the source video, the metric is biased toward the removal target. The inference prompt ('Remove the [dog] in the video', Fig. 1) also differs from the caption used for scoring. Mask quality relies entirely on SAM2 with no manual verification reported.

Efficiency comparison is not apples-to-apples: baselines run at 5B/13B/14B parameters (CogVideoX-5B, HunyuanVideo-13B, Wan2.1-14B) while BridgeRemoval uses Wan2.1-1.3B, so the 'favorable balance between quality and efficiency' claim conflates model size with method efficiency.

Presentation problems: duplicated equations between Sec. 3.2 and Sec. 4.2 (Eqs. 3-4 vs 9-10), inconsistent baseline naming (Senoria/Senorita/Señorita), typos ('leading to leading to incomplete object erasure'), and key ablations, limitations, and VBench results relegated to the appendix while the main text repeats the overclaiming.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of video object removal as video-to-video translation via a stochastic bridge, using the source video as a structural prior instead of Gaussian noise. This directly addresses the paper's identified limitation of noise-to-data diffusion (incomplete erasure, implausible content).

Technically reasonable integration of DDBM/VP-SDE bridge with a frozen VAE and DiT backbone; the dual-role conditioning (source latent as both bridge prior and spatial condition) and the velocity-matching training pipeline are clearly described.

Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) is a simple, intuitive FiLM-style mechanism to relax the bridge prior in large masked regions while preserving background fidelity. Qualitative ablation (Figure 4) demonstrates its benefit for a large bus removal.

Strong empirical results: best or second-best on most metrics across DAVIS and BridgeRemoval-Bench, e.g., PSNR 28.22/33.24, MSE 133.36/46.35, CLIP-F 0.9768/0.9917, and competitive runtime (1.111 s/frame). The improvement of 1.64 dB PSNR on the new benchmark is notable.

User study with 24 participants and 1440 evaluations shows consistent preference for BridgeRemoval over ROSE, VACE, and GenOmnimatte across textual consistency, background fidelity, and temporal consistency.

The new BridgeRemoval-Bench (150 videos, landscape/portrait, single/multiple objects) and captions for DAVIS are useful community resources. The paper also includes an honest limitations discussion and an impact statement on misuse risks.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is not rigorous. Appendix B.1 asserts that Eq. 10's coefficients are derived from a VP-SDE but only states the mapping from DDBM's general coefficients under an unproven condition ('This equality holds if we define...'). Appendix B.3 claims equivalence to score matching but defines a residual ε_res and then equates vθ to it, while the actual target u_t is a different combination of ε and z_tgt; the algebra does not establish the stated equivalence. The method may still work empirically, but the claimed theoretical grounding is shaky.

Reproducibility is limited. The inference SDE solver weights w1,w2,w3 in Eq. 14 are not specified; the variance schedule σ_t and its relation to β_min/β_max are not defined; the exact integration points/layers for AMM are not described; and no code release is mentioned. These omissions make exact reimplementation difficult.

Quantitative evaluation does not measure inpainting quality in the masked region. PSNR/MSE/LPIPS are computed only on unmasked areas, so they do not assess the synthesized content where the object was removed. CLIP-T/CLIP-F are coarse proxies, and CLIP-F values are nearly indistinguishable across methods. For synthetic Veo data, ground-truth clean videos could have enabled masked-region metrics, but none are reported.

The AMM ablation is only qualitative (Figure 4). There is no quantitative ablation table isolating AMM's contribution to PSNR, LPIPS, CLIP-T, etc., so the central claim that AMM balances background fidelity and generative flexibility is not quantitatively supported.

Benchmark construction has inconsistencies and unclear data provenance. The contributions claim 'meticulously annotated masks,' but Sec. 5.1 states masks are generated using SAM2 for all 150 videos. For real-world Pexels/TikTok videos, the target/clean videos and the source of the 'object removed' captions are not described, making the CLIP-T evaluation protocol unclear. Licensing/privacy for TikTok/Pexels data is not discussed.

Comparison fairness and reporting are incomplete. Baselines are evaluated off-the-shelf while BridgeRemoval is trained on ~47k pairs including ROSE; it is not stated whether baselines were retrained on the same data. Runtime is reported on vague 'L20X GPUs' without resolution or batch size. Some baselines are arXiv preprints (Senoria, Ditto, ICVE), and their evaluation settings may differ.

The real-world composite training data uses SAM2 foregrounds composited onto clean backgrounds, which can introduce boundary, shadow, and lighting artifacts; Qwen3-VL filtering is mentioned but not detailed. This may limit real-world generalization and is not analyzed.

Minor presentation issues: typos such as 'leading to leading to' (Sec. 1), inconsistent notation (σ_t vs \barσ_t, z_tgt vs z_0), and unclear use of 'VP-SDE' for a schedule that is not derived from a standard VP-SDE.
